opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me it starts with stepping back from the way the field has framed itself for a long time, which is around building an individual intelligent agent, a single brain in a box that we try to make as smart as possible and then measure against humans. That's a fine research goal, but it's not really what's happening when these systems go out into the world. What actually happens is that they become part of large collections of people, institutions, data flows, and other algorithms. They're embedded in markets, in medicine, in transportation, in finance. Once you see that, the right unit of analysis isn't the single agent; it's the system, the ecosystem.

Economics has been thinking about that kind of thing for a couple of hundred years. How do you get good collective outcomes when you have many participants, each with their own goals, their own private information, their own incentives? How do you design mechanisms so that people want to participate, tell the truth, and share value fairly? Those are exactly the questions that come up when you deploy learning systems at scale, and our field has mostly ignored them. We tend to treat the data as if it fell from the sky, a fixed distribution we sample from, when in fact the data comes from people who are reacting to the system, who have strategic reasons to behave one way or another, and who often aren't being compensated for what they contribute.

So an economic perspective means taking incentives, scarcity, information asymmetry, and fairness seriously as first-class design concerns, alongside accuracy. It means thinking about producers and consumers, about how value flows, about contracts and mechanisms. A concrete example I like is music. A recommendation system can be thought of purely as a prediction problem: predict what this listener wants. But you could also think of it as building a two-sided market that connects musicians with listeners, so that the musicians actually get paid and can make a living. That's a very different design, and it creates a healthier ecosystem over time.

And there's a statistical side to it as well, which I care about a lot. When decisions are being made at scale, you need to handle uncertainty properly. You need to know when the system is likely to be wrong, you need calibrated error bars, and you need to think about decisions and their consequences, not just predictions. Statistics, economics, and computer science together give you that. Each alone gives you a piece.

So to me the ecosystem view is less about making a super-intelligence and more about engineering. It's like building chemical engineering or civil engineering, a discipline for designing large systems that serve people well, are robust, are fair, and create value for all the participants, not just the people who own the platform. That's the real challenge, and frankly it's a more exciting and more humane one than the "build a brain" framing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses collective outcomes, incentives, participation, and fair value sharing, but it does not identify improving both cooperation and competition among agents as a purpose.

r002.rationale: It discusses fairness and incentives, but does not say technology should help people avoid harming others while pursuing their own agendas.

r003.rationale: It says AI systems are embedded in collections of people, institutions, data flows, and algorithms, and identifies the system or ecosystem as the right unit of analysis.

r004.rationale: The music example says a system could help musicians earn a living, but the response does not advocate evaluating AI by the human work opportunities it creates.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. So let me start with what I think is the wrong framing, which is the one that's dominated the field for the last decade or so, and that's the framing of AI as a single intelligent entity. The image is of a brain in a box, something that's smart the way a person is smart, and the whole project is to make that thing smarter. And I've never found that compelling, either as science or as engineering.

When I look at what's actually been built, and what's actually been valuable, it's not a single intelligence. It's a system. It's data flowing from millions of people, being aggregated, being turned into predictions and recommendations, and then flowing back out to millions of people who make decisions on the basis of it. That's a collective. It's much more like a market or a transportation network or a supply chain than it is like a mind. And once you see it that way, the questions change.

So an economic perspective, for me, means a few things. First, it means taking seriously that these systems are made up of many agents with different goals, different information, and different incentives. The people providing data have interests. The people consuming recommendations have interests. The platform in the middle has interests. And they're not aligned, and no amount of making the model in the middle more accurate fixes that. You need mechanisms, in the economist's sense. You need to think about who's getting what in exchange for what, and whether the arrangement is one people would actually agree to if they understood it.

Second, it means caring about scarcity and about value creation. The reason markets are such a remarkable technology, and I do think of them as a technology, is that they allocate scarce things in a decentralized way without anyone needing to know everything. Nobody is in charge of getting bread to Paris every morning, and yet it happens. I think that's a far better model for what we want from large-scale intelligent systems than the central planner model, which is essentially what a giant monolithic model trained to do everything amounts to. And a lot of my recent work has been on exactly that, on recommendation systems and matching markets where you want to allocate attention or goods and there's real competition, where if everyone gets recommended the same restaurant, nobody gets a table.

And third, the ecosystem part. Biology gives you this picture of lots of entities coexisting, competing, cooperating, with no single organism that's the point of it all. The health of the thing is a property of the whole. I think we should be asking about the health of our data ecosystems in that spirit. Are they robust? Do they produce value broadly, or do they extract it? Do people have agency within them? Those are the questions I care about, and they're honestly not the questions you ask if you think the goal is to build one big smart thing.

Now, I'm a statistician at heart, so I'll add that there's a deep technical agenda here too. Uncertainty, for one. A market participant who doesn't know how confident to be in a prediction can't make a sensible decision. So the systems have to quantify uncertainty honestly, not just emit a point estimate. And there's the issue of what people want, the preference elicitation problem, which engineering tends to wave away by saying we'll just maximize some objective. But the objective isn't given. It has to be discovered, in interaction, with many people at once. That's a very different intellectual program, and it draws on microeconomics, game theory, mechanism design, and statistics all together.

So the short version is, I don't think the interesting thing happening in the world is that we're building artificial minds. I think we're building the infrastructure for a new kind of economy, one where decisions are being made at scale based on data, and we haven't yet built the discipline, the engineering discipline, for doing that well. That's the thing I'd like to see people work on.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI systems as ecosystems of agents who compete and cooperate, and argues for economic mechanisms that address misaligned interests and make their arrangements workable.

r002.rationale: It discusses participants’ differing interests and incentives, but does not say technology should help people pursue their own agendas without harming others.

r003.rationale: It places AI within a broader data ecosystem and economic system, explicitly contrasting that collective with the model or single intelligence at its center.

r004.rationale: It discusses value creation and human decision-making, but does not evaluate AI by the work opportunities it creates.

astra-6.text:
To me, it means stepping back from the individual machine and asking what happens when you have a whole collection of decision-making systems interacting with people and with one another. What are their objectives? What information do they have? And how do their decisions affect everybody else?

Think about a recommendation system. You can frame it as predicting which item a person will click on. But there are also people producing those items, people trying to earn a living, and a platform deciding who gets access to whom. A recommendation changes the opportunities available to those people. So you're not just making a prediction about a fixed world; you're participating in shaping that world.

That's where economics becomes relevant. It gives us a language for incentives, allocation, competition, and cooperation. Prices are one mechanism, but the broader question is how to organize interactions so that people can discover opportunities and make mutually beneficial decisions. Accurate predictions can help, but accuracy alone doesn't tell you whether you've built a good system.

And the ecosystem perspective means that there isn't necessarily one objective that somebody at the center should optimize. There are many participants with different interests, and those interests evolve. You want to understand whether the system gives useful feedback, whether participants can enter and thrive, and whether it remains stable as they adapt.

So I see a substantial part of the AI challenge as building the principles for these systems of interacting decisions. Machine learning is an essential ingredient, but we also need to think about the institutions and mechanisms within which that learning operates.

r001.rationale: The response connects economics to competition and cooperation, and says interactions should be organized so people can make mutually beneficial decisions.

r002.rationale: It discusses participants’ different interests and the effects of decisions, but does not say technology should help people pursue their own agendas without harming others.

r003.rationale: It explicitly moves beyond an individual machine to a collection of interacting systems and the ecosystem in which they operate.

r004.rationale: It mentions people earning a living and opportunities affected by recommendations, but does not advocate evaluating AI by the human work opportunities it creates.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it starts with recognizing that an AI system doesn’t exist in isolation. You have people producing data, people making decisions, people providing services, and all of them have different goals and different information. The question is how you build a system in which those interactions work well.

A lot of machine learning has focused on a single decision maker: here’s a dataset, here’s an objective, let’s optimize it. That’s useful, but it leaves out much of what makes a real system difficult. If I recommend a route to one driver, that may be a good route. If I recommend that same route to everybody, I’ve changed the traffic. Your decisions affect my outcomes, and mine affect yours. We need to reason about that interaction, not just make better predictions.

That’s where economics enters: incentives, information, allocation, and mechanisms that coordinate people. I don’t mean simply putting a price on everything. I mean asking who benefits, who bears the costs, what information people have, and whether they have reasons to participate honestly.

And the ecosystem perspective means that we shouldn’t imagine one central intelligence doing everything. We should think about many interacting components, with people very much part of the system. The engineering challenge is to make those interactions productive and reliable. Intelligence, in that picture, is as much a property of the system we build together as it is of any individual algorithm.

r001.rationale: It discusses incentives and mechanisms that coordinate people, but does not clearly identify improving both cooperation and competition among agents as a purpose.

r002.rationale: It notes that people have different goals and that decisions affect others, but does not clearly say the system should help people pursue their own agendas without harming others.

r003.rationale: It places AI within a broader ecosystem of interacting components and people, rather than treating it as an isolated algorithm or central intelligence.

r004.rationale: It mentions people producing data and providing services, but does not advocate evaluating AI by the human work opportunities it creates.
